item.description: Sizzle and Sounds Get your friends together, bring a chair and relax by the Noosa River, 2-5pm on Saturday 28 […]
item.content:encoded:
Sizzle and Sounds

Get your friends together, bring a chair and relax by the Noosa River, 2-5pm on Saturday 28 November on the lawn in front of the Noosa Yacht & Rowing Club. The Kombi Van will be serving Squealing Pig wines, can bar available and live music with Maurice Milani. Games, promotional giveaways and a free sausage sizzle.

Tewantin-Noosa RSL Women’s Auxiliary

The final meeting of the Year & our Christmas Lunch will be held on Friday 4 December, with our meeting at 10-30am followed by our Christmas Lunch in the Dining Room.

Cost; $20 members $25 non members. Please bring a gift (unwrapped) for the Salvation Army children’s xmas appeal. Please Ph; Kay 0402804270 to book.

Sea Scouts Fundraiser

This Christmas, buy your real tree from Noosa Sea Scouts and support the youth in our community. Scouting provides young people with opportunities to develop valuable life skills, confidence and teamwork through adventure, outdoor activities and new experiences.

Pre-order your real Christmas tree online at noosascoutxmastrees.com by Friday 27 November. Choose from two collection dates, Saturday 28 November or Saturday 5 December, with delivery also available.

Talks program

U3A noosa Friday Talks are held at 1.30 pm at U3A, 64 Poinciana Ave. Tewantin

Friday 20 November 2026 Darrel Roche – Somerset.

Friday 27 November 2026 Zero Emissions Noosa – Swap the Drive: Can We Make Noosa More Liveable?

Full details available on U3A website www.u3anoosa.com.au/

SUNSHINE COAST PARKINSON’S ACTIVITY GROUP

The Sunshine Coast Parkinson’s Activity Group meets at 10.30am on the third Friday of each month at the Noosa Tewantin Bowls Club, Hilton Tce, Tewantin. The group welcomes people living with Parkinson’s disease and other neurological disorders, as well as their carers, family members, and supporters.

Meetings provide an opportunity to share information, discuss relevant issues and enjoy the support of others. Learn about new developments in Parkinson’s research and things that will help you in your journey.

Guided activities are also available to people with Parkinson’s disease, restricted movement, or voice difficulties. You do not need to be a member of the group to participate.

For further information, contact Kaye on 0428 201 178.

HOST INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS

Sunshine Beach State High School is seeking local families to host international students for six months from January 2027. All you need is a spare room, a welcoming home, and meals for your student. Generous financial reimbursement and ongoing support provided. Interested? phone Sharon Forbes on 54404294 or email sforb23@eq.edu.au

BOTANIC GARDENS NEEDS VOLUNTEERS

The Friends of Noosa Botanic Gardens are on the lookout for enthusiastic volunteers to help maintain our beautiful gardens, learn more about gardening, meet new friends and welcome visitors. If you can spare a few hours on a Thursday morning, your contribution will be greatly valued and appreciated. No prior experience needed – just a positive attitude and willingness to lend a hand. If you’re keen to join us, contact Julie Bartlett (0416 225941) or Willy Ostwald (0417 332787) for a chat.

NORTH TEWANTIN BUSHCARE

Join the North Tewantin Bush Care Group of local volunteers every first and third Sunday of the month from 7.30-9.30am to help maintain the beautiful natural flora in the area. We weed & plant along the river. It is light work and a lot of fun. All equipment is provided and an excellent morning tea follows. Grab a hat and come along. Phone 0432384596.

BOOMERANG BAGS NOOSA

Fabric donations always needed. Boomerang bags are sewn from recycled fabric with the aim of reducing single use plastic bags and minimising landfill from discarded textiles. Any unwanted fabric: doona covers, sheets, denim, curtains or upholstery fabric can be dropped off at Wallace House on a Monday or Wednesday morning. Phone Ned: 0411 784 911. Facebook: boomerangbagsnoosa

CROQUET CLUB

Free ‘Come & Try’ Croquet every Sunday at 08.15am at Noosa Croquet Club 9 Seashell Place, Noosaville. Phone Ed 0402 246 833 or Bob 0421 041 021.

SUNDAY DANCE

Every Sunday, from 12.30pm at the Tewantin Masonic Hall, Moorindil St. We start by teaching basic dance steps, then Waltz, old time, New Vogue, Ballroom Dances and a little Latin. We run to 5pm. Lots of fun and dancing, including a 20 min. tea/coffee break to socialise. (Only $10) Hope to see you there. Guys needed, so men, free lessons for the first six weeks. Singles or couples welcome. Just rock up or phone Andrew 0429 829 328. For more info, please visit andrewsclassdance.com

THE GLORY OF OPERA

Enjoy the music and the artistry of opera live on screen at U3A auditorium at Tewantin with tutor and opera buff Jeremy Martin. Starting at 9.30am on Mondays, Jeremy, using online documentaries, explores the lives and careers of celebrated present and past composers, conductors and singers. We encourage discussion and we have a lot of fun. New members are always welcome and you don’t have to be an opera lover to join. Contact Jeremy on 0406 959 097 or jdm@kaput.com

VIEW CLUB

The Noosaville VIEW Club is a valued part of The Smith Family dedicated to supporting the education and wellbeing of disadvantaged Australian children. On the 2nd Thursday of each month this warm and welcoming women’s club gathers for our “Friendship Day” nosh and camaraderie. On the 4th Thursday of each month we have our club lunch meeting at the Tewantin RSL with a guest speaker and update on our fourteen Learning for Life students. New members and guests are always welcome to come along for fun and friendship.

For more information email viewnoosaville@gmail.com

SENIORS INDOOR BOWLS

If you are interested in a low impact, friendly activity then indoor bowls is for you. We are a group of seniors enjoying the health benefits of interacting with like minded and friendly people. Experience is not necessary and a high standard is not expected. The aim is fun and friendship. We meet every Friday at the Noosa Leisure Centre in Wallace Drive. Arrival time is between 8.30 and 8.45 for a 9am start. Pop in to see how it works or ring me (Pam) on 0407 493 402.

MAGZ JAZZ

Increase strength, flexibility, energy and wellbeing. Dance exercises and stretch. Learn new dance moves and routines to inspired music. Jazz & Latin style dance keeps body moving, mind agile, memory working and spirit lifted. Tuesdays 8am-9.30am in Tewantin. Phone Margaret for details 0425 269 988

JOIN ZONTA CLUB OF NOOSA

For over 30 years, the Zonta Club of Noosa -proudly affiliated with Zonta International – has strived to empower local women through education bursaries, and health initiatives, providing advocacy and support for issues caused by gender-based violence and homelessness. We host fundraising and advocacy events throughout the year. Join us for our monthly dinner meetings.

Visit zontanoosa.org or email admin@zontanoosa.org

HERE’S A NOVEL IDEA

So you want to write a best-seller? Or perhaps you’ve had the idea of a story rattling around your brain forever. If that’s the case, bring your novel ideas or part-written fiction and join us at Noosa Novelists at our meetings on Monday mornings at Wallace House, Noosa, when we read and comment on pre-emailed chapters of each other’s work, offering ideas and suggestions in friendly discussion to help develop our stories. If interested, please email Noosa Shire Arts and Crafts at create@noosaartsandcrafts.org.au and head it ‘Novelists enquiry.’ Please give details of any publications past and present, or work in progress.

COMMUNITY GARDEN

New Members welcomed. We can offer memberships for fit and active individuals, who are eager to participate in our organic vegetable, herb and fruit garden activities on Friday mornings in Noosaville. Call 0416 054 650.

THURSDAY GIRLS

The Thursday Girls is a registered Australian charity, run by a committee of volunteers. We are a group of women who are passionate about supporting children whose families are suffering financial hardship. Local schools apply to The Thursday Girls for grants for individual students. If the application is successful, The Thursday Girls will transfer funds directly to the school to provide the nominated student access to new opportunities and educational resources, such as a school camp or new sports or educational equipment. The committee arranges monthly fundraising lunches (and other events) at local restaurants. Join us and meet others or get your friends together. Contact: Linn 0418 103 008

AUSTRALIAN MOTORHOMING LIONS CLUB

Are you passionate about giving back and supporting the amazing charitable work that Lions Clubs accomplish across Australia? The Australian Motorhoming Lions Club is looking for new members from all walks of life—no camping vehicle required! As a travelling club, we assist other Lions clubs with their projects as we journey from place to place, raising funds and lending a helping hand wherever we go. Join us now, for further information please contact us via email: membership@amlc.org.au, or phone Lynne 0408 366 299

SENIORS SOCIAL GROUP

We welcome singles and couples to join us for coffee and conversation in a warm, friendly atmosphere, with no joining fees, at the Boathouse on the Noosa River, Thursdays, 10am as well as Tuesdays at the Tewantin Marina Wine bar, 10 am. We also have other optional social activities including lunches, dinners, trivia, picnics, live music events etc. Please call Joan on 0419517869 for more information.

CAN LAUGH

We are a small group who meet once a month. We started some years ago as a Breast Cancer Support Group, but over the years we have people who came with other forms of cancer for support, so if you would like to come and have a chat with us we would love to say hello. We meet the first Friday of the month at the CWA Hall, Tewantin 10am to 12noon. Phone Val: 0422 997 781 or 0427 868 163.

GUILDED LILIES

The Guilded Lilies meet on the last Saturday of every month at the Masonic Hall, Moorindal St, Tewantin, 9am-3pm. Come along, meet new friends, learn new skills, enjoy the company of like minded people. All crafts welcome. Phone Angela 0408 068 148

SALVOS MATES SUPPORT

Phone us about our new men’s mental health support group. You may be interested as a bloke who would like a private chat about your wellbeing? Or you have a friend in need? We (SMS) are an all-male group, typically outdoor type retirees. If you are interested as a volunteer, we are particularly looking for men living in the regional towns such as Cooroy, Pomona, Eumundi. Phone Mike, Al, or Peter on 0423 317 375.

NOOSA DAYBREAK ROTARY

If you’ve had a fulfilling career and are interested in ’Giving Back’ to the community, join us at Noosa Marina, Café VinCino. We meet every Thursday at 7:30am for about an hour or so, and breakfast. We are a group of around 24 people who live in and around Noosa. We raise funds and support organizations that assist people in our community. Our current major project, in partnership with the Salvation Army’s ‘First Response Team,’ is helping the homeless transition from sleeping in their cars to leading a normal life. Come and have a chat with us.

NATIONAL SENIORS

Tewantin Noosa National Seniors group meet at Tewantin RSL on the third Thursday of each month at 10.30am. We offer outings, social gatherings, information sharing and friendship. Morning tea is served and we have guest speakers each month who share valuable information with our members. We welcome new members and visitors are also welcome to these meetings. For more information about our group please contact president Colleen Riley 0417 849 473.

BOOK CLUB WITH A TWIST

We are a small and friendly group of adults who like talking and/or listening to discussions about books, authors, illustrators, characters and word choices. There is no prescribed reading that you have to do (that’s the twist!). Just bring along any book that you have read, or are currently reading, to discuss informally. All book genres are welcome. Everyone is welcome. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month at the tables inside Cooroy Library 1pm – 2ish. Completely free. Email contact is bookclubwithatwist@hotmail.com

PROBUS CLUBS

Probus Clubs are designed for fun and friendship in retirement. If you are retired (or nearly) and are open to making new friends through a variety of activities, then Noosa has several Probus clubs.

PROBUS 2010

Noosa Probus 2010 is a great club for retired men and women who love going on bus trips, having coffee, lunches, dinners, weekly walks, yoga, theatre, garden outings and more. Meetings are held at Lawns (Tewantin Noosa Bowls Club) 65 Hilton Tce, Tewantin on the second Tuesday of the month at 9am. Enquiries Win 0481 397 272.

VEGGIE VILLAGE

Veggie Village at Rufous St Peregian Beach is a community garden growing organic fruit, herbs and vegetables. Membership is open to anyone who wants to learn more about gardening, share their knowledge or just make some friends. Veggie Village has individual plots for rent plus communal plots that we look after and share. Contact us on info@veggievillage.org.au or visit veggievillage.org.au

ACTIVITY WITH PARKINSONS

The Parkinsons Activity Group, provides activities for Parkinsons sufferers, the activities range from Boxercise in the Box Office, 25 Project Avenue (0422 485 482) Georgina, Physio-led exercise (0490 444 255) Emily, Speech Therapy voice and choir (0400 037 901) Edwina. Call Ann for an info pamphlett on 0458 009 601. Parkinsons Group meets the third Friday of each month at Noosa Tewantin Bowls Club at 10.30am for information and lunch. You need to stay active and socialise to help deal with the symptoms.

FABULOUS 60S PLUS

We are a fun, friendly, seniors social group. We welcome couples and singles to join us for morning coffee every Tuesday at the Noosa Marina wine bar Tewantin, from 10am and every Thursday at the Boathouse on the Noosa River from 10 am. We also have a monthly program of lunches, dinners, picnics, walks and other fun activities. Contact Joan on 0419 517 869 for more details.

PHOTO CLUB

We meet on the second Monday of each month at Uniting Church Hall, 6 Grasstree Court, Sunrise Beach at 7pm. The club comprises all levels of expertise form novice to professional. The night comprises a guest speaker, supper and our monthly critique of member’s work. Visitors welcome.

BEEF AND BURGUNDY CLUB

Noosa Beefsteak and Burgundy club meet on the third Wednesday evening of the month at a different local restaurant for good food, wine and fellowship. We invite couples or singles to join us. Further information contact John Dicker on 0414 323 266.

FAMILY HISTORY

The Heritage Centre at 17 Emerald Street in Cooroy welcomes visitors to research family and local history. Volunteers are there to help.

Access a wide range of resources including a library, computers, digital databases and subscriptions to MyHeritage, Ancestry.com, FindmyPast and more.

Open Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays 9.30am-1pm Information ph. 07 3129 0356 or visit genealogy-noosa.org.au

MENS SHED

The Noosa Men’s Shed provides a venue for the men of Noosa to gather in an environment of traditional Australian mateship. It aims to advance the health, well being and social inclusion based on individual interests of the members. The Shed also offers facilities and support for many activities: woodwork, metalwork, gardening, arts studio, music, hobbies (leatherwork, technology, amateur radio), health and wellbeing, bee keeping, aquaponics and hydroponics. Membership is $120 per year. Visit the Shed office on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 8-11am at Rotary Lane off Wallum Lane, Noosa Springs.

TOASTMASTERS

We are a supportive public speaking club dedicated to improving your confidence and creativity in a safe environment. Our meetings are every 2nd and 4th Monday of the month, from 6.30-8.30pm at the CWA Hall, Tewantin. The first two visits are free. For more information email noosatoastmasters@gmail.com

TUNE IN TO NOOSA FM

Tune in Noosa FM 101.3 or stream live on noosafm.org for local updates and Great Music for a Great Community. Noosa’s community radio station is committed to developing local talent

item.title: Murder at the golf club
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Local author, Rita Lee Chapman, has just released the third book in her murder trilogy set on the Sunshine Coast, […]
item.content:encoded:
Local author, Rita Lee Chapman, has just released the third book in her murder trilogy set on the Sunshine Coast, Murder at the Golf Club, featuring DI Mark Williamson.

Following on from Murder at the Tennis Club and Murder at the Yacht Club, Murder at the Golf Club is set at a local golf club in the Tewantin area.

“Another murder on the Sunshine Coast!  This time, the body of a local real estate director is found on the golf course. DI Williamson has to decide whether his death was related to his business, his family or his mistress.”

DI Williamson moved to the Sunshine Coast with his wife, Christine, for a quieter lifestyle. But murder isn’t confined to cities. Both the Laguna Bay Tennis Club and the Laguna Bay Yacht Club have been crime scenes and now it is the turn of the Golf Club.

Rita has written fourteen books, featuring mysteries, horses and children’s stories.

On Saturday, 5th December, Rita will be signing books outside Berkelouw Books, Eumundi from 9 am – 12 noon .

Visit her website at www.ritaleechapman.com. Find her books on Amazon at www.amazon.com/Rita-Lee-Chapman/e/B00B5OS2Q4/

item.title: 1956 Melbourne Olympics – but what about the stadium?
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: There’s has been much discussion in recent months about the lack of ‘progress’ about where the Olympic Stadium would be […]
item.content:encoded:
There’s has been much discussion in recent months about the lack of ‘progress’ about where the Olympic Stadium would be the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games. Since the announcement by the International. Olympic Committee (IOC) in January 2021 that Brisbane would host the Games, with the lead-time of eleven years instead of traditional seven years, there has been much discussion, criticism and controversy about whether the Olympic Stadium ‘will be ready’.

This article is not about that query, but about the 70th anniversary celebrations of the Opening Ceremony of the first Olympics held in the southern hemisphere in Melbourne on 22 November 2026. This event was mentioned in last week’s feature in Noosa Today about Australia’s oldest Olympian, 99-year-old canoeist, Bryan Harper; he will be present for the celebratory luncheon in that 1956 Olympic Stadium on Sunday. That venue is, of course, the Melbourne Cricket Ground, better known as the MCG.

In June 1946 the Victorian Olympic Council (VOC) had reserves in the bank of just £6 7s 10d (that is, less than $13) when it reconvened the first meeting in seven years. However, it was proposed at that meeting that Melbourne would develop a bid to host an Olympic Games.

It gained from the support from -Australian Olympic Federation (AOF) now the Australian Olympic Committee (SOC), and from the then Lord Mayor of Melbourne, Sir James Connelly, and significantly, former Lord Mayor Sir Frank Beaurepaire. Beaurepaire’s public profile in Australia and in the Olympic Movement was a key factor in the success of Melbourne’s bid. He had won 3 silver and 3 bronze medals at Olympic Games (1908, 192O and 1924) and had been an official at the 1932 Olympics. Following his return from Los Angeles in 1932 he developed his motor tyre business utilising the brand name ‘Olympic’. Beaurepaire Tyres is still a prominent business.

in January 1948 an extravagant Invitation book, with additional copies bound in either suede or merino lamb’s wool, were sent to all IOC members, international sports administrators and public figures. The book outlined reasons why Melbourne should become an Olympic Games host: Australia was only one of four nations to attend every summer Olympics and consequently it was the senior Olympic country in the southern hemisphere; if the Olympics were truly ‘world’ Games, it was time for them to be held in the southern hemisphere; and, with the development of pressurised aircraft, the thirty hours travel to Melbourne was comparable with other venues.

The story of the bid is of interest but the thrust of this article is to compare and contrast it with the purported difficulties of Olympic Stadiums – 1956 Melbourne and 2032 Brisbane.,

‘Melbourne Gets the Games’ was front page news when it was announced on 30 April 1949.

This should have completed the story of the Melbourne bid, but another headline in the Melbourne Age that day read “Site for Games not yet settled” foretold a possibility that Melbourne came close to losing the Games. Yes, there was much excitement about hosting the Games, but there were many rumblings, especially in relation to the desperate shortage of housing in Victoria at that time. However, a Letter to the Editor of the Age perhaps expressed the positive element in society at the time:

… re The London 1948 Olympics … Despite the shortages, despite the austerity, the war-weary island and its people welcomed the sportsmen (sic) of the world. Can we not do likewise in the same spirit … There is time before the 1956 Games to overcome our chronic housing shortages if we catch the same spirit as Britain and look ahead and reach just a little for the stars.

The strategy of the Melbourne Invitation Committee before ‘decision day’ had been to proceed with anything likely to persuade the IOC to award the Games to Melbourne. The extravagant plans for a new Olympic Stadium and Swimming Pool complex were two examples.

The Olympic Organising Committee vacillated over the site for the main stadium -seven were mooted: The MCG, Olympic Park, Princes Park (Carlton Cricket Ground), Albert Park, St Kilda Cricket Ground, the Showground, the Melbourne University Sports Oval, and the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).

The IOC President Avery Brundage expressed deep concern over the lack of progress. What seems now to have been an obvious choice from the outset – the MCG – was ‘non-negotiable according to the MCG Trustees. A key problem was why would you the biggest stadium for cricket and Australian football be resurfaced, levelled for a cinder track and rendered unusable for two cricket seasons for about two weeks of Olympics?

A third attempt in five years to negotiate for the MCG to become the Olympic Stadium was made with key community, state and federal politicians, including Prime Minister Robert Menzies over the consecutive days. Victorian State Premier John Cain stated clearly he would not provide funds for a ‘new’ stadium in Carlton, but would assist in the renovation of the MCG, including increasing its capacity from 85,000 to 120,000.

However, the day after Brundage visited the MCG in April 1955 (only 19 months before the Opening Ceremony on 22 November), the Melbourne Argus reported that Brundage had seen only five men trying to do the work of 100 because of an industrial dispute.

Brundage lamented that in the six years since Melbourne had been awarded the Games there had been ‘nothing but squabbling, changes of management and bickering’.

At the end of his six-day inspection tour Brundage was quoted as stating that the IOC had made a serious mistake in allocating the Games to Melbourne in 1949. He intimated that, even at that late stage, several other cities (he seemed to favour Philadelphia) would be prepared to stage the 1956 Games.

Brundage’s scathing criticism seemed to work; it galvanised action and greater co-operative effort among the individuals, committees, and agencies during those final eighteen months of preparation.

Olympian Bryan Harper and many others will share many recollections over lunch at the 70th Anniversary at the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Stadium on Sunday. Known ever since as the ‘Friendly Games”, Melbourne’s struggle with deciding on the Olympic Stadium may not even rate a mention.

However, there will be much interest and discussion in what transpires in relation to the Olympic Stadium in the ‘few years’ leading to the 2032 Brisbane Games.

[Dr Ian Jobling was Founding Director of the UQ Centre of Olympic Studies and is now Honorary Patron of the Queensland Centre of Olympic and Paralympic Studies. ]

item.title: Last wave at school
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: St Andrew’s Anglican College Year 12 departing surf team gathered on Peregian Beach at 6am for some final waves, in […]
item.content:encoded:
St Andrew’s Anglican College Year 12 departing surf team gathered on Peregian Beach at 6am for some final waves, in uniform, marking their last day of school and upholding what has become one of the college’s most-loved traditions.

Fellow St Andrew’s surfers lined the sand forming a guard of honour with boards raised as the team of 2026 ran toward the ocean, watched by class mates, parents, grandparents and teachers.

Many of the students had been in the college surf team since Year 4 or 5 and were happy to finish school the way they spend their weekends, surfing together.

College principal Karen Gorrie said the class of about 130 seniors had had an amazing year, with lots of achievements and lots for the kids to be happy about.

The traditional final surf kicked off a “big day” for the students that included a special assembly and graduating dinner.

Ms Gorrie said the students future ambitions were quite diverse. Some were going into university, “into every course you can imagine,” with the health sciences a popular choice. Many others planned to start their apprenticeships for trades and some were taking a gap year to head overseas or work here and save for future plans, she said.

Parents said the last day of school brought them a mix of excitement for the future ahead and sadness for the end of a chapter.

Many students in the class were planning to spend their Schoolies week in Bali and several of the mothers, calling themselves “Moolies”, said they would be going with them.

Graduating students across Noosa schools marked their final day with a traditional run into the ocean.

item.title: Love letter to the unseen
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Spencer Hitchen’s passion for the environment began as a small child and he was just 6 years old when he […]
item.content:encoded:
Spencer Hitchen’s passion for the environment began as a small child and he was just 6 years old when he joined the Bird Observers at Noosa Parks Association. He became particularly concerned about the vulnerable glossy black-cockatoos he observed and their home in the wallum ecosystem which was being threatened by development. His campaign to protect this local wallum gained international attention when, at the age of 10, he launched a petition which attracted almost 86,000 signatures.

Since then, Spencer has taken his campaign well beyond the Sunshine Coast, and his environmental journey is now the subject of a global documentary ‘Love Letter to the Unseen’. This documentary film follows Spencer on his journey of discovery to understand the imminent threats to the endangered Maugean skate and the intrinsic beauty of a species that exists in a world unseen by many.

Spencer declares, “It has been incredible to be asked by Emmy award-winning director Josh ‘Bones’ Murphy to be in this film that follows my conservation journey and how I learnt about the Maugean skate in Tasmania. ‘Love Letter to the Unseen’ is about biodiversity loss from a youth perspective. It’s an incredibly hopeful, impactful, powerful and inspirational film for all.”

Come along to Friday Environment Forum on November 27 to view the documentary with Spencer and hear how this film has become an inspiration for others to take action for conservation.

Stay after the forum for our end-of-year lunch.

Everyone is welcome at the Noosa Parks Association Environment Centre, 5 Wallace Drive, Noosaville at 10-10.25am (morning tea available), 10.30 am (forum begins).

Entry is $5 by ‘tap & go’ but Noosa Parks Association current members are free.

Join the Bird Observers at 8.30am in the carpark for interpretive birding.

For more info: www.noosaparks.org.au

item.title: Crafting for a cause
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Over the last six years, the Australian fibre arts community has united to raise $257,000 for breast cancer research after […]
item.content:encoded:
Over the last six years, the Australian fibre arts community has united to raise $257,000 for breast cancer research after Knit for the Girls was kicked off in 2020, as an annual fibre community fundraiser by Karina Moore of Louie and Lola Yarns.

Each year yarn stores, knitwear and crochet designers and yarn dyers, have donated hundreds of skeins of yarn, books and accessories for raffle prizes for the campaign.

Noosaville yarn store owner Sarah Price decided to take their fundraising efforts to the next level.

Through her yarn store, Say! Little Hen, Sarah hosted a creative morning tea for local crafters, with all proceeds going to the Knit for the Girls Campaign.

“Usually, as a sponsor of Knit for the Girls, we provide donations for the raffles, but I thought we have such a beautiful community of women here, it would be great to come and see if we could do more,” Sarah said.

It’s hard to find a member of the fibre arts community who hasn’t been impacted by breast cancer, be it personally or through a family member or friend, with 1 in 7 women in Australia diagnosed with breast cancer in their lifetime.

“We’ve got a few customers who have been impacted by breast cancer, so it’s great to be able to come together with our craft and raise money for such important research,” Sarah said. “We did a pink-themed morning tea, with flowers kindly donated by Kate at Eumundi & Co to decorate the shop. A few of the ladies also chipped in to help, bringing along home-baked cakes and treats, and also providing the beautiful pink party plates. It’s been a challenging year for a lot of people; coming together reminds us we’re not alone and we can do amazing things when we support each other.”

All proceeds from the ticket sales went to the National Breast Cancer Foundation, while Sarah also created a special pink collection of yarn kits, with 10 per cent of proceeds going to the cause.

“So many of our customers are sprinkled around Australia and wanted to be able to contribute more,” she said. “Most donate to the main campaign by joining in the raffles – by creating a special collection with 10 per cent of sales going to the National Breast Cancer Foundation, our customers were able to shop and contribute to a good cause. I wasn’t sure how much we’d raise from our small business but I was blown away by what we can achieve when we come together. I’m excited to say we raised $945 in total for the National Breast Cancer Foundation, which is far more than we expected.”

Last year, additional sponsor activity contributed over $9,000 in donations raised for the Knit for the Girls Campaign. This year, this exploded to $30.4K directly from sponsor activity.

item.title: Kawana Waters wins the big one
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Tim Ryan BP OAM, Sunshine Coast Branch president, proudly congratulated Kawana Waters Surf Life Saving Club on behalf of us […]
item.content:encoded:
Tim Ryan BP OAM, Sunshine Coast Branch president, proudly congratulated Kawana Waters Surf Life Saving Club on behalf of us all, for being named DHL Australian Club of the Year, at the Surf Life Saving Meritorious Awards in Sydney.

Being named Australia’s leading surf lifesaving club is the highest accolade of all. It is an achievement for the whole Sunshine Coast Branch to celebrate, not just the Kawana Waters community.

Tim said: “This prestigious national recognition reflects the remarkable culture, leadership, dedication and commitment within Kawana Waters SLSC.” He noted that the branch’s 15 outstanding affiliated clubs, each contribute to the strength and success of surf lifesaving across the region.

“To see one of our own recognised at the highest level nationally, is an exceptional moment for the Sunshine Coast, and a testament to the calibre of our clubs and the people who lead them.”

Behind every great club is an incredible community of people, who give their time, energy and passion to something bigger than themselves. Kawana Waters exemplifies the very best of what sure lifesaving stands for – a commitment to saving lives, developing people, strengthening communities and creating opportunities for generations to come.

As president of the Sunshine Coast Branch he extended his sincere congratulations to all members and the wider club community. “You have put the Sunshine Coast ton the national stage, and you should be immensely proud.”

Shaw and Partners Iron Series – round 2&3

Round 2&3 of rpt Shaw and Partners Iron Series was held on the weekend at Thirroul NSW with Noosa Heads Surf Life Saving athletes Finella Gibbs-Beal and Electra Outram both competing.

Friday – Repechage round: the weekend kicked off on Friday with the repechage round giving the bottom 10 athletes, following the Coolangatta Gold a second chance to qualify for the series. The top four athletes progressed while the series came to an end for the remaining six competitors. Noosa’s Finella Gibbs-Beal battled hard across three 12-minute races, improving with each round. Unfortunately, Finella narrowly missed the top four cut off.

While disappointed not to progress, the experience has given Finella plenty of motivation and made her hungry to return for next year’s series.

Saturday – Round 2: Enduro Format. Electra Outram was next up for Noosa on Round 2 on Saturday. This format suited Electra perfectly being her favourite race format. Coming off the back of her victory at the Coolangatta Gold, Electra carried plenty of confidence into the race.

Electra led for most of the race with the result coming down to a sprint finish off the final ski against Lana Rogers. Lana eventually clinched the win with Electra finishing a very close second.

Sunday – Round 3: Sprint Format – brought a tougher sprint format, with Electra competing strongly against the field. With three rounds now completed, Electra sits in second position overall in the Shaw and Partners Iron Series.

She heads into Rounds 4&5 in Newcastle in January in a strong position. The next event on the calendar is the Hayden Kenny Classic, hosted by Alexandra Surf Life Saving Club on 27-29 November.

This weekend, Alexandra Headlands hosts an Australian Surf Rowers League Queensland (ASRLQ) surf boat carnival. Noosa will field two under 19 crews, one male and one female, who are keen to gain experience. The under-19s will be swept by Stuie Cooper. Noosa will also enter a reserve grade crew, swept by veteran Mick Gardner.

In the gym their weights program will be under the guidance of veteran coach Woogie Marsh. Once again, it will be good to see the boat section of Noosa consolidate and move on. Formed in 1949 this section has had good crew, and being a team sport (crew of five – one sweep and four rowers) it is always good for teamwork and club spirit. A big welcome to a new young boat week in Noosa, Brendan Reily-Cush who has the art of boat sweeping on his ming.

Pickleball in Noosa

Recently the Noosa Pickleball club held a very successful twilight “Monster” event which involved 48 players on 12 courts at the one time. Our flyer informs us, that held on the Noosa district netball courts at Tewantin, under the lights, there were eight teams of eight players, who all played eight doubles games. Teams were encouraged to embrace the theme of the fun event and dress in the colours of their teams. Teams were also encouraged to have an even match of players for all ranks, players from beginner to advanced, all playing together.

President Nick Noosa said: “we had the green team with Shrek ears, yellow team had a special well-dressed man, pink team had a very pink lady and our club mascot, “Dinky”, the bush turkey, was not left out either. Bragging rights for this inaugural event went to the white team, who narrowly won by one point”.

“This was a truly special event for us as a club. We are so thankful to the Noosa netball club and Noosa Council, for their support and assisting us to create a great social and sporting event for our members. We already have players wanting Ito put their names down for the next one. When you include our members who prepared the courts, rant the events and kept all running smoothly, we had over 50 members, all having a great time.”

Noosa Pickleball Club runs free “Come and Try” lessons with can be booked on their website. This is a sport that should be given as much support as is possible, as it caters for not only the very young, but also those who have been through the years and are now enjoying their twilight time.

As the great Pavarotti once said: “There are two things in life that belong to the people: music and sport”. So who’s up for Pickleball?

Martial Arts

Another Noosa champion is on the rise. At just 18, Sophia Ennis has made her mark internationally in Shotokan Karate. In the first weekend of November she competed at the 12th Karate Commonwealth Championships in Glasgow, Scotland, where she won the silver medal in the U21 Kumite (Sparring) and a bronze medal in the Senior Kumits (sparring).

This is a massive result for this 18-year-old superstar. Back in October she won the World Shotokan Karate Federation (WSKF) National in Adelaide and was also promoted to 2nd Dan, by Japanese instructor Tara Kasuya. Sophia now has eyes set on being one of Australia’s best and the way she is going she will soon achieve her goal. This speaks ever so highly of the standard o coaching she receives from her sensei Bryan Dukas, 6th Dan; also a well done to the coaching panel of Karate Noosa. This is a sport in which discipline and fitness is of the upmost importance.

item.title: Priority development declared at aerodrome
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: The State Government last week declared Caloundra Aerodrome a Priority Development Area, unlocking a $78.1 million expansion of the Sunshine […]
item.content:encoded:
The State Government last week declared Caloundra Aerodrome a Priority Development Area, unlocking a $78.1 million expansion of the Sunshine Coast’s HeliMods, delivering more than 10,000 square metres of defence-grade aerospace infrastructure and strengthening the state’s defence and aerospace supply chain.

The government claims the move will support 150 construction jobs and creating about 100 ongoing high-skilled operational jobs.

The milestone expands on the government’s $31.65 million investment in HeliMods in June 2026, the first funding recipient under the flagship $180.6 million Sovereign Industry Development Fund.

HeliMods is one of only a few Australian companies delivering end-to-end aerospace capability across design, certification, advanced manufacturing and systems integration.

The Priority Development Area is designed to unlock the broader potential of Caloundra Aerodrome, creating opportunities to attract further investment, grow the aerospace and defence industries and deliver more jobs for the Sunshine Coast.

The declaration will not affect the continued operation of the Caloundra Aerodrome, which will remain the responsibility of Sunshine Coast Council or existing tenants, a government spokesperson said.

“Economic Development Queensland will work closely with the local community, existing businesses and stakeholders, including the Heritage Museum, to ensure their interests are protected and existing operations can continue uninterrupted,” the spokesperson said.

To support the precinct’s growth, an Interim Land Use Plan is now in place while Economic Development Queensland prepares the longer-term Development Scheme for the area.

The proposed Development Scheme will be open for public feedback for 30 business days before it is finalised.

“Declaring Caloundra Aerodrome a Priority Development Area will cut through unnecessary red tape and fast-track the infrastructure needed to unlock a $78.1 million investment in Queensland’s sovereign aerospace capability,” Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said.

“We want to unlock the full potential of Caloundra Aerodrome by creating a platform for the next generation of Queensland aerospace and defence businesses to invest, innovate and grow right here on the Sunshine Coast.

Sunshine Coast Mayor Rosanna Natoli said the declaration was an important milestone for the precinct and an exciting step forward for our region, with high-value jobs and new industry opportunities to be created.

“We look forward to working with the Queensland Government on those priorities, while continuing to represent the interests of our local community,” she said.

HeliMods website says the business was founded in 2002 by Australian entrepreneur, Will Shrapnel – a qualified engineer, pilot, aircraft technician and businessman. “What started as a one-man operation has grown to now become a leading enterprise, with world-renowned, vertically-integrated capability in advanced digital design, engineering, manufacturing, certification, integration and support of aircraft mission systems.”

Mr Shrapnel said the declaration of Caloundra Aerodrome as a Priority Development Area was an important step towards seeing sovereign industry investment realised at the aerodrome, both for HeliMods and for other aerospace businesses.

“We thank the Deputy Premier and the Crisafulli Government for their continued commitment to helping realise sovereign industry investment at Caloundra Aerodrome, and for supporting the Sovereign Industry Development Fund investment with a planning framework to help progress it,” he said.

“We also want to thank Member for Caloundra Kendall Hatcher for her ongoing support of the aerodrome and it’s importance to the broader community.

“Caloundra Aerodrome has a long aviation history and a strong community of operators, and we look forward to working with the Queensland Government, Economic Development Queensland, Sunshine Coast Council and our fellow aerodrome businesses so the precinct grows in a way the whole region can be proud of.”

Further information regarding the Caloundra Aerodrome PDA is available via Economic Development Queensland’s website [LINK], with the community encouraged to register via EDQ’s Have Your Say page to participate in the future public notification phase.

item.title: SharkSmart drone program changes down to trial results
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Local Noosa working party Oceans for All (OFA) renewed its call for the Queensland Shark Smart drone program to be […]
item.content:encoded:
Local Noosa working party Oceans for All (OFA) renewed its call for the Queensland Shark Smart drone program to be expanded to seven days a week and for the full day to put Queensland swimmers first.

Formed in 2023, Oceans for All (OFA) is a working party of representatives from multiple groups with a shared goal: to replace and update the Shark Control equipment in the Noosa area with modern technology that protects both humans and marine life.

The recent Noosa Triathlon saw the unprecedented cancellation of the swim leg for the first time in the event’s 40-plus-year history due to significant shark activity off Noosa Beach. More than 8,000 competitors were affected after lifeguards made the precautionary decision to cancel the 1.5km swim leg and prioritise public safety.

Oceans For All Noosa says the event highlights the important role that drone surveillance plays in helping lifeguards make informed decisions and keep beachgoers safe, exposing serious limitations in Queensland’s current half day weekend and holiday only SharkSmart drone program.

The shark activity was first identified on Saturday afternoon, the day before the event, not by the SharkSmart drone program, but by a Surf Life Saving helicopter conducting a routine patrol after drone operations had already ceased for the day.

On race morning, it was local lifeguards who took the initiative to commence drone surveillance earlier than the scheduled drone operation hours currently set by the Queensland government. Their decision quickly confirmed that significant shark activity remained in the area and provided the information needed to make an informed safety assessment.

An Oceans For All Noosa spokesperson said the incident demonstrated the value of real-time monitoring technologies. “The technology worked, but the system around it did not,” the spokesperson said. “If local lifeguards had simply followed the drone standard operating hours set by the government, this shark activity may not have been detected when it was. The reality is that people stepped up on their initiative and operated outside the normal program to ensure beach users were protected.”

The Queensland Government’s SharkSmart drone program currently operates under restricted hours and days of operation which is only half days each Saturday, Sunday and holidays. “What happened at Noosa wasn’t the result of the system working as designed, it was the result of experienced local lifeguards using their initiative and local knowledge to fill a gap in the system.”

The organisation is calling on the Queensland Government to expand the program to dawn to dusk, seven-day coverage with greater operational flexibility, similar to arrangements in New South Wales.

“It’s about ensuring that the technology taxpayers are funding can be used when and where it is needed, putting Queensland swimmers first, rather than being restricted by operating hours that don’t always reflect real-world conditions.”

The spokesperson said the Noosa Triathlon demonstrated the value of drone surveillance and the professionalism of local lifeguards, who continued monitoring local beaches throughout the week. These actions highlighted gaps in the current program.

“The lesson from this event is not that our beaches are unsafe. The lesson is that early detection works, informed decisions work and properly resourced drone surveillance can further strengthen community safety.”

A Department of Primary Industries (DPI) spokesperson said subsequent to Noosa Triathlon event organisers, in consultation with SLSQ, cancelling the swim portion of the event following shark sightings on Saturday and Sunday morning, DPI, in collaboration with SLSQ, made the decision to schedule five additional days of drone flights at Noosa as part of the Shark Smart drone program.

“The SharkSmart drone program is a beach safety partnership funded by the Queensland Government and delivered by Surf Life Saving Queensland (SLSQ),” the spokesperson said.

“The Queensland Government is investing in innovation as part of the SharkSmart drone program including extended visual line of sight, beyond visual line of sight and drone-in-a-box technologies. If successful, these technologies may allow for increased spatial and temporal drone coverage at program locations.

“The department will not consider changes to the operating arrangements of the SharkSmart drone program in Noosa until the outcome of these advanced technology trials is known.

“The SharkSmart drone program is a key initiative under Queensland’s Shark Management Plan 2025–2029 and complements other shark mitigation measures in the Shark Control Program.

“Under the plan, shark-spotting drones will continue to be rolled out to additional beaches and become a permanent feature of operations.”

The spokesperson said the department regularly reviews program performance and emerging technologies to ensure Queenslanders have the most effective suite of shark safety measures.

Oceans For All Noosa has again invited the Minister for Primary Industries to meet with local stakeholders to discuss opportunities to strengthen the SharkSmart drone program and build on the success of existing shark mitigation measures.

item.title: Travelling the Nile in style
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Viking has announced its new 19-day Grand Nile Journey itinerary exploring Egypt is now open for booking. With departures beginning […]
item.content:encoded:
Viking has announced its new 19-day Grand Nile Journey itinerary exploring Egypt is now open for booking.

With departures beginning in 2028, the new itinerary offers Viking’s most in-depth exploration of Egypt to date, featuring four hotel nights in Egypt’s capital and a 14-night sailing between Cairo and Aswan on board the all-suite Viking Ra.

Guests will discover the country’s renowned landmarks alongside lesser-visited archaeological sites and communities in Middle Egypt, gaining a deeper understanding of the history, culture and traditions that have shaped life along the Nile.

“Egypt has captivated travellers for generations, and we believe there is always more to discover,” Viking Chief Executive and President Leah Talactac said.

“At Viking, we design our itineraries for curious travellers who want to gain a deeper understanding of the places they visit. Our new Grand Nile Journey reflects that approach, giving guests more time to explore Egypt and experience the many layers of its history and culture.”

The new Grand Nile Journey itinerary features 17 guided tours designed to provide a more comprehensive exploration of the country’s significant history and traditions.

Guests will begin in Cairo, where highlights include the Great Pyramids of Giza, the Great Sphinx and the Grand Egyptian Museum, before continuing along the Nile through the heart of Egypt.

Among the voyage’s distinctive experiences are visits to sites throughout Middle Egypt that offer a fascinating perspective on the country’s ancient civilizations.

Guests will discover the Meidum Pyramid, which represents an important chapter in the evolution of pyramid construction. They will also explore the cliffside Noblemen’s Tombs of Beni Hasan, renowned for their depictions of daily life in ancient Egypt.

At Tell el-Amarna, guests will encounter the remains of the once-lost royal capital established by Pharaoh Akhenaten, while a visit to Deir el-Muharraq monastery offers insight into Egypt’s Coptic Christian heritage and the site traditionally associated with the Holy Family’s journey through the country.

Continuing south, guests will experience the grandeur of ancient Egypt at the temples of Luxor and Karnak, the royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Seti I at Abydos.

The journey also includes time in Aswan, where guests can explore the island temple complex of Philae, immerse themselves in Egypt’s storied past during a visit to the monolithic temples at Abu Simbel and sail the Nile in a traditional felucca. Throughout the voyage, scenic sailing reveals the contrast between the Nile’s lush green riverbanks and the surrounding desert landscapes.

For guests wishing to extend their travels, Viking is offering pre and post land extensions that can be seamlessly combined with the Grand Nile Journey itinerary.

Options include Cairo (two nights; with services of a Viking Host), offering more time to discover Egypt’s vibrant capital; Morocco (five nights; fully guided), showcasing its colourful markets and rich heritage; and Jordan—Dead Sea, Petra and Amman (four nights; fully guided), highlighting ancient wonders and dramatic landscapes.

For additional information, visit www.viking.com.

item.title: Looking after yourself Noosa style
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Living in Noosa gives us plenty of reasons to stay active. Walking, swimming, surfing, golf, cycling, gardening and enjoying the […]
item.content:encoded:
Living in Noosa gives us plenty of reasons to stay active. Walking, swimming, surfing, golf, cycling, gardening and enjoying the outdoors are all part of a healthy lifestyle. But staying active is only part of the equation. Our bodies and minds also need time to recover.

As we age, regular recovery can become increasingly important. Taking time to relax can help us manage the everyday effects of busy lives, physical activity and stress, while helping us feel refreshed and ready to keep doing the things we enjoy.

There are a number of simple ways to make recovery part of a healthy routine.

Massage can provide welcome relief for tired, tight or overworked muscles. Infrared sauna offers warmth and relaxation, providing time to unwind after exercise or a busy week. Float therapy takes relaxation a step further, providing a quiet, low-stimulation environment where the body is supported in warm, salt-rich water and there is very little to do except stop and switch off.

These are some of the wellness experiences available at Noosa City Cave, where the focus is on giving people dedicated time to relax, recover and look after themselves.

Of course, wellness doesn’t need to be complicated. Good food, regular movement, quality sleep, social connection and appropriate health care remain the foundations of living well. Treatments that encourage relaxation and recovery can complement those habits.

As we get older, perhaps the goal isn’t to slow down. It’s to look after ourselves well enough to keep doing the things we enjoy.

City Cave Noosa – 2/11 Gibson Road, Noosaville, phone 39242787. www.citycave.com.au
